transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for calling S-Net technical support. My name is Toby. How can I help you today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hello Toby. I'm calling because my internet ping spikes from twelve milliseconds up to three hundred milliseconds every few minutes while I'm playing online games. I am connected via a direct Cat 6 Ethernet cable directly into port 1 of the router.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I can certainly look into those latency fluctuations for you. Can you please confirm the S-Net broadband account number printed on your welcome letter?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, the account number is ACC-884-9102.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you Zain. And what is the hardware serial number from the sticker on your S-Net Hub 5?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The serial number is SN-HUB5-88319. Toby, I am competing in the European regional esports qualifiers this Friday with a fifteen thousand pound prize pool! If my ping spikes during the match, my character freezes, I get eliminated instantly, and my entire team gets disqualified! I've spent six months training ten hours a day for this, and I am literally on the verge of a panic attack!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let us check the line transmission sync and latency buffers on our network monitoring console.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, please tell me what you see.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: So if I have understood correctly, you are experiencing severe packet latency spikes up to three hundred milliseconds during competitive gaming sessions despite using a direct Cat 6 Ethernet connection, and you need the ping stabilized to prevent game dropouts during your upcoming tournament matches. Is that right?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, exactly. When nobody else is home, the ping is 12ms, but when anyone else does anything online, it shoots up to 300ms instantly.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Looking at your optical ONT connection at the exchange, your physical fiber line has zero packet loss and a steady nine hundred megabit downstream sync.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So the fiber line itself is not physically dropping?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The physical fiber link is entirely healthy. The symptom you are describing is bufferbloat, which occurs when router packet buffers fill up during concurrent traffic bursts.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Bufferbloat? What exactly is that?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: When an upload or download saturates your connection, standard router queues hold packets in a large FIFO buffer, introducing queuing delay that inflates gaming round-trip latency.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That explains why it happens whenever my brother uploads a video to YouTube or my sister streams Netflix in 4K!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: We will configure Smart Queue Management and Quality of Service priority rules inside your S-Net Hub 5 to prioritize gaming traffic packets above bulk data.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: How do we access those QoS settings in the hub?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Open your web browser and navigate to 192.168.1.254, then log in using your admin credentials.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Navigating to 192.168.1.254... typing the admin password... I'm on the main Hub Manager overview page.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Click on Advanced Settings in the left sidebar, then select Traffic Management.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Advanced Settings... Traffic Management. I see Quality of Service, Bandwidth Limiter, and DSCP Tagging.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Click on Quality of Service, and toggle 'Enable Smart Queue Management' to ON.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Toggling Smart Queue Management to ON. Several input fields have unlocked for Upstream and Downstream bandwidth limits.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Under Upstream Bandwidth, enter 105000 kilobits per second, which represents roughly ninety percent of your provisioned one hundred and fifteen megabit upload rate.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Typing 105000 in Upstream. Why do we set it to ninety percent instead of one hundred percent?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Capping traffic at ninety percent ensures the bottleneck queue remains inside the router where fq_codel scheduling can discard buffer backlog, rather than letting the modem queue saturate.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That makes complete mathematical sense. What about Downstream Bandwidth?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Under Downstream Bandwidth, enter 820000 kilobits per second to keep downstream buffers completely clear under heavy family loads.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Entered 820000 in Downstream.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Now click on 'Priority Devices' tab within the QoS menu.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Clicking Priority Devices... I see a list of connected devices with MAC addresses.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Locate your gaming PC's MAC address and set its Traffic Priority class to 'Real-Time Highest'.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Selected my desktop workstation... set to Real-Time Highest. Clicking Apply Settings.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The hub is recompiling the packet scheduling trees; the status bar will reload in twenty seconds.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The page refreshed and displays 'Smart Queue Management Active - fq_codel algorithmic scheduler running'.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Now let us run an online bufferbloat test at waveform.com/tools/bufferbloat from your gaming desktop.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Opening the Waveform bufferbloat test page... clicking Start Test now. It is testing unloaded ping, download active ping, and upload active ping.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Observe the 'Active Ping' numbers while download and upload saturate the bandwidth.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The results are in! Unloaded ping is 11ms. Download active ping is +2ms, and upload active ping is +1ms! Total score is an A+ grade!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: An A+ bufferbloat rating confirms latency variance under maximum saturated load will not exceed two milliseconds.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: From +300ms down to +2ms! That is an astounding improvement, Toby!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Obviously that confirms packet queue prioritization is operating within optimal millisecond parameters, Zain.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Now let me launch Counter-Strike 2 and join a European competitive warmup server to test in-game telemetry.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Go ahead, let us inspect live in-game network telemetry.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Connecting to Frankfurt server... net_graph shows 14ms ping, 0% packet loss, and zero jitter! It feels completely butter smooth!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let us also check your DNS server configuration on your computer to ensure query lookups are expedited.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Where should I verify the DNS resolver?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Under your Windows Ethernet adapter properties, verify IPv4 DNS is set to 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1 for Cloudflare Ultra-Low Latency.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Checking Ethernet properties... set primary to 1.1.1.1 and secondary to 1.0.0.1. Clicking OK.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Cloudflare provides sub-two millisecond DNS query resolution for European gaming master servers.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That shaves another couple milliseconds off every server connection handshake.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let us also check your network card's Energy Efficient Ethernet toggle to prevent micro-sleep packet pauses.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Under Configure Network Adapter, Advanced tab... Energy Efficient Ethernet is listed. Should I disable it?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, disable Energy Efficient Ethernet and Green Ethernet so the PHY controller remains powered at maximum clock speed.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Disabled both Green Ethernet and Energy Efficient Ethernet. Done.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Now let us verify DSCP packet marking for your voice communication client so team Discord calls don't interfere with gameplay.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, our team uses Discord voice channels constantly during tournaments. How do we ensure voice packets get priority?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: In Discord settings under Voice and Video, enable 'Quality of Service High Packet Priority', which attaches DSCP 46 expedited forwarding tags.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Toggling Quality of Service High Packet Priority to ON in Discord settings. Done.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The S-Net Hub's fq_codel engine recognizes DSCP 46 and schedules voice packets ahead of bulk TCP streams.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That prevents our team voice communications from crackling or dropping during intense skirmishes.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let us also check the MTU packet size under WAN settings on your hub to confirm optimal frame transmission without fragmentation.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Under WAN Settings, MTU is set to 1500 bytes. Is 1500 bytes ideal for S-Net Full Fibre?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, on our IPoE DHCP full fibre architecture, an MTU of 1500 bytes allows maximum frame payload without packet fragmentation overhead.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I will leave MTU locked at 1500 bytes then.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Just to check, Zain, is your landline telephone and general household WiFi functioning properly as well?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, my family's tablets, smart TVs, and phones are browsing perfectly without any interruption.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I will remain the dedicated owner for this support case and record the SQM fq_codel profile on your customer record.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you so much Toby. You have literally saved our team's tournament prospects this weekend.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Ensure you restart your router once every six months to refresh internal memory tables.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I will set a calendar reminder to do that regularly.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Is there anything else regarding your S-Net broadband or gaming latency that I can assist you with today, Zain?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, that has resolved my latency completely. Thank you Toby.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: You may receive a short customer satisfaction survey by SMS after this call; we would appreciate any feedback on your experience today.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'll give you five stars on the survey. Good afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for choosing S-Net, Zain. Best of luck in your tournament qualifiers, and take care.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you, goodbye.
